GEN. TAYLOR AND THE SABBATH SCHOOL SCHOLARS.

Yesterday morning, more than a hundred of the girls attached to the Sabbath school of St. Matthew's Church, assembled in that place, and performed the ceremony of crowning the Queen of May. They were all arrayed in white, and on their heads were wreaths of flowers, and in their hands bouquets. It was a spectacle on which the eye dwelt with delight. At noon, preceded by their pastor, the Rev. JAMES DONELAN, and in accordance with previous arrangement, they walked to the White House, to pay their respects to the President. Having arranged themselves to the best advantage, Mr. DONELAN made brief address, introducing Miss TAYLOR, who was the floral sovereign of the occasion. She advanced, and presented to the President a beautiful bouquet, with appropriate remarks, to which he responded by expressing his pleasure that the honor had been conferred upon a namesake, and wishing them all the happiness that the choicest blessings of Providence can bestow. We regret that we were not present, but the friend from whom we received this information speaks of the scene in terms of enthusiasm, and as one rejecting the highest credit on the scholars, and adding another evidence of the amenity of manners and the kindness of heart which, not less than his prowess in the field, distinguish the illustrious chieftain.


1.—THE DISGRACEFUL SPECTACLE.—


This is the title of an article under the editorial head in Tuesday's Union. Although intended to apply to the conduct of General TAYLOR, it is a fit caption to the slander which succeeds it. "When fighting the battles of his country," the writer remarks, "General TAYLOR exhibited the noblest virtues of the soldier and the finest traits of humanity. Now, notwithstanding the most solemn pledges, to the contrary, he becomes the revengeful despot, and the ruthless proscriber of his countrymen, who hated not him, but the party which had opposed their country, but which, for the most selfish purposes, supported him for the office to which he aspired."

is execrated in Scotland for the barbarous
atrocities of 1745, not lustrous by royal patent
but by the endowments of his mind, the gift of
Heaven itself [Why did not the silly people make
him President?—Ed. Here] whose fame fills
the world at this moment—he whose magnificent
and overpowering eloquence has so often charmed
his eager listeners—he at the sound of whose voice
the dungeon has yielded up its victims—he who
has led in the Senate of his country, when it was
composed of men who would have reflected lustre
upon Athens when it was in the height and full
splendor of its political, national, and literary
glory—he who in the forum convinces juries,
astounds the judges, and delights the hearers—he
who in foreign countries has with dignity, and
an ability never surpassed, and very seldom
equaled, represented his own, insisted upon her
rights in all their plenitude, and upheld her pre-
rogatives—he, say, is at this queen of watering
places—the magnet which attracts the attention of
all, and the respect and deference of all [Why did
not the silly people make him President?—Ed. Here]

Saratoga is honored with the presence of one of the
greatest men, not only of this country but of the
age in which he lives. His fame is universal as
the mighty and almost matchless strength of his
mind is unquestioned and unquestionable. It is
not my province to speak now of his politics—they
have not, in my opinion, anything to do with his
consummate genius. [Why did not the silly people
make him President?—Ed. Here] His politics, at best,
rank; and in the affairs of State, and it is one of the
highest privileges of men to differ from
each other. [Why did not the silly people make
him President?—Ed. Here] But pettifoggers, trad-
ing patriots, designing and selfish politicians,
querulous, and petulant and disappointed office seekers,
attempt to argue in opposition to this view of the
question. Henry Clay is well known; no descrip-
tion of his person, no praise of him, is required;
and for me to compliment him, or to pronounce
a eulogium upon him, would be like to the tyro in
sculpture attempting to amend the work of Prax-
iteles. [Why did not the silly people make him Pre-
sident?—Ed. Here] But there is always something
to be said about a great man—it is a never-falling
theme. Genius shows itself in so many forms that
the notice of it must be frequent. The country is
always anxious to hear of the movements of such
persons, as it has deep interest in their health and
happiness. [Why did not the silly people make him
President?—Ed. Here] Henry Clay is the pride and
glory of this land, and I think that those who see
matters through different medium, are ready to
admit that he is so: His genius is the inheritance of
sixteen millions of people, richer one than even,
according to himself, he had. It is consoling to
know that thousands can worship at the shrine of
genius, without reference to its possessor, graced
by learning of the most profound and varied charac-
ters and associations. [Why did not the silly people
make him President?—Ed. Here] Henry Clay has his
faults and his foibles, and has imperfections, and so
has every great man; it is the lot of human nature.
The late Lord Kenyon was so ardent an admirer
of, and so much attached to, that accomplished
orator, Lord Erskine, whose speeches are among
the most beautiful and chaste productions of our
language, that when speaking of the imperfections
of the latter (Lord Kenyon) would say that the
sun itself had spots upon it; and in that style he
invariably answered the calumnies of those who
saw in that illustrious man nothing but his faults,
the invariable conclusion of treacherous and das-
tardly minds. [Why did not the silly people make
him President?—Ed. Here] This is the first time
I have had an opportunity of seeing Harry of the
West, as he is sometimes familiarly designated, and such title is nobler and more
honorable than that of prince, duke, marquis or
earl, because we all know how very many of those
have been got, viz:—for the commission of acts at
which justice stands fighting and humanity itself
trembles. [Why did not the silly people make him
President?—Ed. Here] What ahead Mr. Clay has!
What laboratory therein—what powers of
origination, what facilities for thought—what
scope, range and play for ideas, in each of which
is comprehended a whole subject, and with what
kind determination nature assesses the supremacy
of her work to the last—for her child, her orna-
ment, her pet still retains his faculties in all their
strength and grandeur. [Why did not the silly
people make him President?—Ed. Here]

Several populations have waited upon him to re-
quest the honor of his presence in their different
locations; but as he has come here for the benefit
of his health, which is in a rather delicate state,
he does not intend to incur the fatigues of public
life; and, under the circumstances, we think he is
perfectly right. This morning a deputation from
Troy, composed of some of its most respectable
citizens, waited upon him for the purpose of ten-
ding to him the hospitalities of that city. He
received them with his usual courtesy and urba-
nity, and having thanked them most cordially for
the honor they had conferred upon him, declined
to accept the invitation. To the deputation from
Albany he returned the same answer. He says
that he will be most happy to see every one who
calls upon him, and if the waters agree with him
he will remain here for a fortnight. Wherever he
is a crowd collects round him, and each one lis-
tens with breathless attention to what falls from
his lips. He is accompanied by his son, James B.
Clay, and his family, and grandson, a fine little
fellow, between twelve and thirteen years of age,
the son of the late Henry Clay, Junr., who fell
in the service of his country. The lady of the
family is a person of extremely interesting appearance, and of simple and refined manners.
The great man lodges at his private lodgings, but visits the hotel
at the course of the day. The banquets presented brilliant spectacle to-day. This
evening there was soirees in the new ballroom, and
this evening there will be a grand ball, which is
expected to be numerously attended. All the

to make sales.


The Maine Farmer says:- We believe all the
iron works in Maine, and they are very few indeed,
have suspended operations. So what iron we work
up among us comes from abroad. We suppose the
immediate cause of their suspension of operations, is
because the demand is limited, sales slow and prices
very small. At the same time, thousands and thous-
ands of tons are daily coming across the Atlantic to our shores; and for which we have to pay
cash. We are not now going to complain of this
state of things, but will merely express hope
that it will not always continue, but that at some
future day, not only the iron works that have been
built, but many more which will be built, will all
find constant employment.


The last Danve Democrat contains the follow-
ing paragraph, and further testimony, against the
pernicious doctrines of Free trade, as exhibited in
the practical results of the Tariff of 1816:
"Another of the large furnaces of the Montour
Iron Company at this place, blown out on Fri-
day last, leaving but one of their four furnaces in
operation. The reason assigned is the low price of
iron and the slim prospect of any immediate improve-
ment. The Company has large quantity of iron
still on hand, which will keep their Rolling Mill
going for some time. No stability in the iron bus-
iness can be expected under the ad valorem system
of the Tariff of 1816. Without the substitution of
specific duties, our Iron Works must drag on a sick
existence, subject to the caprices of English manu-
facturers, who regulate the prices."


What Merchant should be:- A merchant should
be an honorable man. Although a man cannot be
an honorable without being an honest man,
yet a man may be strictly honest without being honor-
able. Honesty refers to pecuniary affairs; honor re-
fers to the principles and feelings. You may pay
your debts punctually, you may defraud no man, and
yet you may act dishonorable. You act dishonor-
ably when you give your correspondents a worse
opinion of your rivals in trade than you know they
deserve. You act dishonorably when you sell your
commodities at less than their real value, in order
to get away your neighbours' customers. You act
dishonorably when you purchase at higher than
the market price in order that you may raise the
market upon another buyer. You act dishonorably
when you draw accommodation bills, and pass them
to your banker for discount if they are out of
real transactions. You act dishonorably in every
case wherein your external conduct is at variance
with your real opinions. You are dishonorable when,
carrying prosperous trade, you do not allow your
servants and assistants, through whose exertions you
obtain your success, to participate in your prosperity.
You act dishonorably, if after you have become
rich, you are unmindful of the favors you received
when poor. In all these there may be no
intentional fraud; it may not be dishonest, but it is dishonorable.

Further news in the Straits

The steamship Canada arrived at Halifax on Monday evening bringing seven days later news from Europe.

Official notice of the intervention of Russia in Hungary has been received in Paris. The number of men placed at the disposal of Austria is said to be 4,000. Accounts from India report the entire termination of the war on the Punjab.

FRENCH AID TO ROME.—It was reported that troops were to leave France for Rome. It was reported that those under Gen. Cudinot had reached that place, and that the Romans had risen in favor of the Pope, that Mazzini and the Republican Government had fled. The Pope would be compelled not only to grant an amnesty, but desirable reforms.

DEFEAT OF THE AUSTRIANS.

The Hungarians have beaten the Austrians, and have almost driven them out of the country.

The greatest alarm prevails at Vienna and has had the effect to reduce Radetzky's demand on Piedmont from 12,600,000 francs to 50,000,000 francs.

It is said that the Tuscan troops had entered Leghorn, and that the Sicilians, beaten at all points, have virtually submitted to the King of Naples.

The Markets.

Mark Lane, MAY 5.—Another feeling of depression has come over the Grain trade. The weather has lately become very favorable to the growing crops which causes buyers to confine their purchases to immediate wants. At Mark Lane on Monday last, English wheat sold generally at decline of one shilling to two per quarter. Foreign wheat also met a very limited demand, although a similar deduction was accepted. On the following day at Liverpool, a limited demand for wheat and flour was experienced, and firmer prices were maintained. Indian corn was in brisk request, and regained the depression last noticed. Indian meal sold at 1s per Dbl. yesterday.

mines, I have seen no occasion for the use of arms
of any kind. Let revolvers alone, for my observa-
tion here convinces me that generally they are
quite as dangerous to the assailant as the assailed.
Comparatively few are accustomed to small arms
of any kind and two serious accidents have, to
my knowledge, happened within a fortnight from
the careless use of revolvers. Few are able in mortal combat to be perfectly cool and
well possessed in the moment of danger or strife,
and none who have not entire self-possession
should trust themselves revolvers. One tent,
of the size and description of those used by army
privates, sheet iron tea-kettle, half gallon coffee
pot, frying-pan, axe, saw, hammer,
and assorted nails to every three or four men, or
to each man, if alone and unassociated.


If emigrants come by the Panama route, it will
be better to buy cooking utensils, tools, and hard-
ware of all kinds in San Francisco, than to saddle
themselves with the expense and trouble attend-
ing the transit of the Isthmus. The time will
come, very soon after their arrival in San Francis-
co, when they must shoulder their own pack or
pay extraordinarily for having it done by somebody
else. It is therefore important that their outfit
weigh as little and occupy little space as possi-
ble, and to this end I have omitted everything in
the previous list not absolutely necessary. Single-
handed adventures must inevitably fare worse
when it comes to shoulderng their traps than
parties, because the tent, and some of the impe-
diments &c., are the same for one or for several.


Arrived at San Francisco, if they wish to go to
the North to the diggings on the American River
and its tributaries, they will take launch, or boat,
and go up the Sacramento to Sutter Fort. If to
the Mokelumne or the northern side of the Stanis-
laus, they will go by similar conveyance to
Stockton. On the southern side of the Stanis-
laus, or the Tuolumne, or any river south, they
will take a launch for the Tuolumne landing.
Having reached one or other of these landing
places, beef and hard bread they may need on their
way thence to the mines, and look about for teams
bound for the diggings. Probably they will find
one and a successful will in all probability be
requested to pay $50 per 100 lbs for the transporta-
tion of their goods and chattels to the mines. This
they had much better pay than buy a horse which
will be necessary if no teams are to be found.
A horse will cost $50 and will pack 200 lbs. When
they reach the mines, they will, unwise, sell the
beast, if they get $10 more than $50 for it,
because it will pretty certainly stray or be stolen
the first night. They should take time to look
about the diggings and see how the gold is obtained,
then go to work and open holes for themselves, and,
if they do not the first week make more than
their expenses, they should not lay it to heart.
A mechanic can home satisfied work several years
at his trade before he receives journeyman's wages,
and gold-washing is as much an art as anything
else though it may be learned in much less time
than some others. In a week or two, if not very
stupid, they will understand it as well as their
neighbors, and if with industry and economy they
are not able to go home, at the end of two years,
buy a farm, take Dinah, or Sally, if they like
that name better for it, and she is willing, live com-
fortably the balance of their days—then,
I am no Yankee, and can I guess.

TUESDAY, Sept. 1, 1849.

MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS.—The Board Of Aldermen were in session this evening till late hour—occupying the Assembly Chamber while their own is at last undergoing repairs.

Resolutions were adopted to light the following streets with gas: Ninth, between First Avenue and Avenue A; Avenue A itself through its whole extent. Various petitions for the illumination of other portions of the City were referred as usual.

In answer there was the following action: Gaslight, per recommendation of the appropriate Committee, in Twenty-seventh St. from Third to Lexington Av.; in Third St. from the Bowery to Avenue A; in Tenth St. from Second to Fourth Avs.; Greenwich St. from North to Rector; and Eleventh St. between Sixth and Seventh Avs. Gaslight in Amos St. from Sixth Avenue to the Hudson River was ordered as follows, and referred to Committee for action. In Fourth St. from Lafayette Place to Sixth Avenue to be extended in Forty-second St. and in Seventeenth St. between Second and Third Avs.

A remonstrance presented against the extension of Pier No. 7 was referred to the Committee on Wharves, Piers and Slips.

Engine Co. 5 was petitioned to be reinstated to service. Referred.

In the recommendation of the Finance Committee, some were appropriated for the proposed Fountains; various other business was accomplished which will be found elsewhere under the appropriate heads. At 11 o'clock the Board adjourned for want of a quorum, to meet again one week from today.

THE FIRE DEPARTMENT.—A communication was presented to the Board of Aldermen at their last sitting from the Engineers and foremen of the Fire Department, stating that the spirit of rowdyism is unfortunately growing a serious evil which, if not promptly checked, will result in much difficulty, suggesting such action on the part of the Common Council as shall arrest all these misdemeanors. The Committee who speak on behalf of the firemen offer another suggestion that fine and imprisonment shall be the punishment to any person who shall be found at lacking fireman while in discharge of his duty; but, in correlation, they likewise assert that the delinquents are allowed by the Police to walk abroad entirely unpunished after warrants have been placed in their hands. They complain also of the power sometimes exercised by magistrates in taking the punishment of the offenders entirely into their own hands. The matter referred to the Committee on the Fire Department, we trust, will report some definite plan of improvement.

CROTON AQUEDUCT DEPARTMENT.—The Finance Committee of the Common Council, to whom was referred the subject of the late Judgment obtained against the Department by Mr. Herman L. Edgar, have made Report recommending that further litigation cease and the claim be paid out of any unappropriated balance standing to the credit of the Water Fund; the amount to be charged to the construction of the Croton Aqueduct.

The officers of the Department have asked for an additional appropriation of $1,000 to meet the expenditures arising from the collection and arrangement of the statistical Tables pertaining to the Department, required by the law of April 11, 1849.

POTTER'S FIELD.—The Committee on Laws of the Board of Aldermen, have made Report with Communication from the Corporation Counsel, relative to the legality of purchasing Remsen Island for a Potter's Field. The Counsel seems to decide that a burial ground is not a public nuisance and that the land in question is properly within the Jurisdiction of the City and consequently governed by its laws. Whether the report of the Committee or the opinion of the Counsel gives any decisive ruling on the subject, the report from the Special Committee having the matter in charge.

MORGAN RESULTS OF THE RIOT.—Numerous اخبار of this unfortunate affair are continually coming up in the Board of Aldermen. Last evening there were claims to the service of some officer, a bill for $700 being for medical services for Policeman Burley who was seriously injured by the rioters. These demands took the course of their predecessor—reference with power. The claims growing out of the Riot already count thousands, when shall we hear the last of it?

FOURTH WARD CONTESTED ELECTION.—The Special Committee of the Board of Aldermen on the contested seat for Alderman of the Fourth Ward have reported in favor of the sitting member, AID Mullins. After examining the claims of Archibald Hall, Esq., the opposing candidate, the Committee say that although some irregularities have been proved which should not have occurred, they do not alter the result and hence conclude that to-present Alderman is fully qualified for his seat.

PUBLIC BUILDINGS.—The extension proposed has again been defeated at least for the present in the Board of Aldermen. On Monday evening, AID Scherrer passed resolutions providing for the purchase of the Old Arsenal property, for the sum of $75,000, the Commissioners of the Land Office being to receive it; but the matter was laid upon the table.

THE TEN GOVERNORS.—At the last meeting of the Board of Aldermen communicated to them from the Ten Governors relative to certain needed repairs for the buildings under their care—the President offered a resolution to see the attendance of such repairs to the Commissioner of Repairs and Supplies, but that expenditures under said head be charged to the proper account.

REMOVAL OF CITY OFFICIALS.—A resolution to remove the corps of the inspectors from office was discussed in the Board of Aldermen on Tuesday. Two members only voted in the negative.

A Special Committee of the Board of Aldermen, of which Mr. Morgan is Chairman, has been appointed to inquire into the propriety of preserving part of ground for Prospect Park in the Seventh Ward.

THE carrying about of tied dogs is becoming a fashionless occurrence, with cords around the neck. We sometimes see the same business with which we were once acquainted, and since the laws of the contrary are passed.

perty, and also for the purpose of obtain-
